scenes.say: Openhere. Pick an empty space anywhere on the map, and design it for the people who actually live around it.
Pick a spot, and Openhere finds real spaces nearby. Here, a cleared-out Dollarama in Parkdale, Toronto.
scenes.caption: Pick a real space on the map

scenes.say: An agent asks Qloo about the neighbourhood: the moods and decor locals rate, the venues they love, and the artists they would pay to see. Fifteen calls, adapting as it goes.
scenes.caption: An agent asks Qloo who goes out here

scenes.say: Every question starts from that point on the map. Qloo's demographics check each design idea against the local crowd, and its popularity filter sizes the bookings to a six hundred and fifty person room.
scenes.caption: Qloo, from one point on the map

scenes.say: Then it redesigns the real photo, keeping the walls, the windows and the camera, so the before and after is believable. This is Dollar Store Sessions.
scenes.caption: The real photo, redesigned

scenes.say: It books the room from what locals already love: Yukon Blonde, Matt Mays and Jenn Grant, acts small enough to fill it.
scenes.caption: Booked from what locals love

scenes.say: Every design choice cites the Qloo signal behind it, and ideas that draw a different crowd, like cozy or energetic, are dropped.
scenes.caption: Every choice cites Qloo

scenes.say: Ask a language model alone for the same room, and none of its eight picks hold up for this crowd. Three, like salvaged aisle shelving, are not in Qloo at all.
scenes.caption: Without Qloo, 0 of 8 hold up

scenes.say: For a brand, it measures the fit with a fanbase. Red Bull and Phoebe Bridgers fans score thirty six out of a hundred, so the room leans on what both already love: Fender, Vans and Big Red Machine.
scenes.caption: Brand meets fanbase, measured

scenes.say: And then you walk inside. A live world model streams the redesign in real time, from the same photo.
scenes.caption: Walk inside

scenes.say: Openhere. Design the place for the people around it.
